title: Monitoring Employees Doesn't Improve Performance
paragraphs: More and more companies are using technology to monitor their employees, from tracking their computer activity to recording how much time they spend on different tasks. But a growing body of research suggests that this kind of surveillance does not actually make people work better.

One of the most important pieces of evidence comes from a meta-analysis, a study that combines the results of many earlier studies, by a team of researchers led by Ravid and Behrend. It found no evidence that electronic monitoring improved employees' performance. However, it was consistently linked to higher levels of stress among workers. A 2025 review of research on employee monitoring reached a similar conclusion, finding little to suggest that electronic surveillance improves performance.

A 2026 study from the University of Queensland in Australia found another problem. The researchers surveyed 283 employees in the UK working in 23 industries. They found that when employees were closely monitored, they tended to neglect any tasks that were not being tracked. At the same time, the measured tasks did not receive any extra attention. According to the researchers, this suggests that surveillance can harm workers' motivation.
Monitoring may also damage trust. A 2024 study of more than 3,500 workers in Canada linked feeling watched at work to more pressure and stress, as well as less independence and privacy.

However, the evidence is not completely one-sided. A 2024 study of remote workers on the online platform Upwork found that the productivity of the best-performing workers fell by nearly 20% after they were allowed to turn off monitoring software. This suggests that, in some cases, monitoring may have some benefits.

Monitoring can also be useful for other reasons, such as safety, following rules and regulations, or detecting technical problems. Overall, though, the research suggests that companies hoping to improve performance should think carefully before increasing surveillance, since it may raise stress and reduce trust without delivering the results they expect.
